```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(hypergraphs)
```

A corpus is a set of documents, each a set of words. The documents and the
words form a bipartite structure, which is a hypergraph in either
orientation. With documents as nodes, every word is a hyperedge over the
documents that contain it. A word such as *telescope* joins a few documents,
and a word such as *challenges* joins many. Weighting each word by its tf-idf
in each document keeps the difference between the two in the hypergraph.

The corpus here is `covid_abstracts`, 165 abstracts of COVID-19 education
research published between 2020 and 2024. The hypergraph is clustered with
the Laplacian of the random walk with edge-dependent vertex weights (Hayashi
et al. 2020), and a few labelled abstracts are spread to the others by the
label spreading of Zhou et al. (2006).

## From corpus to hypergraph

The abstracts are tokenized, function words and a few words common to all
research abstracts are removed, and the words that occur fewer than three
times in the corpus are dropped.

```{r construct}
stops <- c(
  stop_words_en(),
  "using", "used", "use", "based", "results", "study", "research",
  "paper", "article", "findings", "data"
)

hg <- text_hypergraph(
  covid_abstracts,
  column = "abstract",
  id = "doc",
  weight = "tfidf",
  stop_words = stops,
  min_count = 3L
)
hg
```

```{r construct-values, include = FALSE}
edge_sizes <- hg_measures(hg, what = "edges")
corpus_summary <- hg_measures(hg, what = "summary")
participation <- subset(corpus_summary,
                        measure == "pairwise_participation")$value
```

The hypergraph has `r hg$n_nodes` documents and
`r format(nrow(edge_sizes), big.mark = ",")` words. The median word occurs in
`r median(edge_sizes$size)` abstracts, and the most common word occurs in
`r max(edge_sizes$size)` of the `r hg$n_nodes`. Its tf-idf weight is small
in every abstract.

```{r summary}
hg_measures(hg, what = "summary")
```

The pairwise participation is the share of pairs of abstracts that share at
least one word. It is `r sprintf("%.3f", participation)`, so the hypergraph
is connected and the spectral methods apply to the whole corpus.

## Central words

With words as nodes, two words are close when they occur in the same
abstracts. The clique centrality of a word is its eigenvector centrality in
the projection of this hypergraph.

```{r words}
word_hg <- text_hypergraph(
  covid_abstracts,
  column = "abstract",
  id = "doc",
  nodes = "word",
  weight = "tfidf",
  stop_words = stops,
  min_count = 3L
)
word_centrality <- hg_centrality(word_hg, type = "clique", sort_by = "clique",
                                 n = 10)
word_centrality
```

The most central words are those of the shared subject of the corpus,
education during the pandemic: `r paste(head(word_centrality$node, 7), collapse = ", ")`.

## Clusters of abstracts

`type = "random_walk"` clusters the abstracts by the Laplacian of Hayashi et
al. (2020). The tf-idf weights become the edge-dependent vertex weights of a
random walk, the eigenvectors of its normalized Laplacian place the
abstracts, and k-means divides them. The number of clusters is set to four
and compared with three below.

```{r cluster}
clusters <- hg_cluster(hg, k = 4, type = "random_walk", seed = 1)
aggregate(node ~ cluster, data = clusters, FUN = length)
```

```{r cluster-years}
merged <- merge(clusters, covid_abstracts, by.x = "node", by.y = "doc")
cluster_years <- aggregate(year ~ cluster, data = merged, FUN = mean)
cluster_years
```

The mean publication year of the clusters lies between
`r sprintf("%.1f", min(cluster_years$year))` and
`r sprintf("%.1f", max(cluster_years$year))`, so the clusters divide the
abstracts by subject and leave the years mixed.

The clusters for four and for three clusters are compared below.

```{r sensitivity}
clusters_3 <- hg_cluster(hg, k = 3, type = "random_walk", seed = 1)
hg_agreement(clusters, clusters_3, what = "table")
```

```{r sensitivity-values, include = FALSE}
cross <- hg_agreement(clusters, clusters_3, what = "table")
kept <- function(label) max(subset(cross, label_x == label)$n)
size_of <- function(label) sum(subset(cross, label_x == label)$n)
```

Two small clusters keep their members: `r kept("Cluster 1")` of the
`r size_of("Cluster 1")` abstracts of the first and `r kept("Cluster 3")` of
the `r size_of("Cluster 3")` of the third stay together. The largest cluster,
of `r size_of("Cluster 4")` abstracts, is divided among the three clusters,
so its boundary depends on the number of clusters.

## Classification from six labels

Label spreading (Zhou et al. 2006) gives labels to a few nodes and spreads
them over the hyperedges to the others. The three alphabetically first
abstracts of 2020 are labelled `"early"` and those of 2024 `"late"`.

```{r classify}
labels <- c(
  "2-s2.0-85085897904" = "early",
  "2-s2.0-85087124472" = "early",
  "2-s2.0-85087646998" = "early",
  "2-s2.0-85107489479" = "late",
  "2-s2.0-85112557152" = "late",
  "2-s2.0-85113355756" = "late"
)
predictions <- hg_classify(hg, labels = labels)
predicted_years <- merge(predictions, covid_abstracts,
                         by.x = "node", by.y = "doc")
aggregate(year ~ predicted, data = predicted_years, FUN = mean)
```

```{r classify-check}
hg_agreement(predictions, covid_abstracts, label = c("predicted", "year"),
             what = "table")
```

```{r classify-values, include = FALSE}
unlabelled <- subset(predicted_years, is.na(label))
unlabelled_early <- nrow(subset(unlabelled, predicted == "early"))
unlabelled_2020 <- nrow(subset(unlabelled, year == 2020))
```

Of the `r nrow(unlabelled)` unlabelled abstracts, `r unlabelled_early` are
classified `"early"`, although `r unlabelled_2020` of them are from 2020.
The vocabulary of the corpus changes little between 2020 and 2024, so six
labels do not date the abstracts.

## PageRank, the dual hypergraph and a null model

The PageRank of the random walk with edge-dependent vertex weights (Chitra
and Raphael 2019) uses the tf-idf weights of the hypergraph. The abstracts
with the highest PageRank share words with many others.

```{r pagerank}
hg_pagerank(hg, sort_by = "pagerank", n = 3)
```

A `personalized` vector restarts the walk at chosen documents, which ranks
the abstracts by their closeness to those documents. The dual hypergraph
exchanges the roles of nodes and hyperedges, which gives the word
orientation without tokenizing the corpus again.

```{r dual}
dual_hypergraph(hg)
```

A null model shows whether a statistic exceeds what the degrees of the
nodes and the sizes of the hyperedges imply. The swap null rewires the
binary memberships by checkerboard swaps that keep both (Gotelli 2000). The
test below uses the abstracts of 2020.

```{r null-test}
abstracts_2020 <- text_hypergraph(
  subset(covid_abstracts, year == 2020),
  column = "abstract",
  id = "doc",
  weight = "tfidf",
  stop_words = stops,
  min_count = 3L
)
null_2020 <- hg_null_test(
  abstracts_2020,
  statistic = c("pairwise_participation", "avg_jaccard"),
  n = 99,
  seed = 1
)
null_2020
```

```{r null-values, include = FALSE}
pp <- subset(null_2020, statistic == "pairwise_participation")
aj <- subset(null_2020, statistic == "avg_jaccard")
```

The pairwise participation is `r sprintf("%.3f", pp$observed)`, and the
null reproduces it (p = `r pp$p_value`): abstracts with many words share
words with almost every other abstract under any rewiring that keeps the
degrees. The mean Jaccard index between words is above the null
(z = `r sprintf("%.2f", aj$z)`, p = `r aj$p_value`). Words occur in the same
abstracts more often than their frequencies imply, which is the
co-occurrence the clustering divides.

## Input from quanteda or tidytext

A data frame in long format with one row per document and word is the
incidence structure of the hypergraph, so the output of other text
pipelines can be passed to `group_hypergraph()`.

```{r bridge, eval = FALSE}
# quanteda: tidytext::tidy() turns a dfm into a long table with columns
# document, term and count
group_hypergraph(
  tidytext::tidy(my_dfm),
  node = "term", hyperedge = "document", weight = "count"
)

# tidytext: word counts in long format (document, word, n)
group_hypergraph(
  my_word_counts,
  node = "word", hyperedge = "document", weight = "n"
)
```

## Choice of method

- `hg_cluster()` finds groups without labels. With tf-idf weights,
  `type = "random_walk"` uses them as the edge-dependent vertex weights of
  the walk.
- `hg_classify()` spreads a few labels to the other documents. The `margin`
  column measures the confidence of each prediction.
- `hg_centrality()` ranks the words of a corpus (words as nodes) or its
  documents (documents as nodes).
- `hg_measures()` reports the sizes, overlaps and connectivity that decide
  whether spectral methods apply.

## References

Chitra, U., & Raphael, B. J. (2019). Random walks on hypergraphs with
edge-dependent vertex weights. *Proceedings of the 36th International
Conference on Machine Learning*, PMLR 97, 1172-1181.

Gotelli, N. J. (2000). Null model analysis of species co-occurrence
patterns. *Ecology*, 81(9), 2606-2621.

Hayashi, K., Aksoy, S. G., Park, C. H., & Park, H. (2020). Hypergraph random
walks, Laplacians, and clustering. *Proceedings of the 29th ACM
International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management*, 495-504.
<https://doi.org/10.1145/3340531.3412034>

Zhou, D., Huang, J., & Schölkopf, B. (2006). Learning with hypergraphs:
Clustering, classification, and embedding. *Advances in Neural Information
Processing Systems 19*.
